newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Mir rescue crew due for start on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Russian Mir rescue crew due for start on Tuesday.

text.p: A two-man Russian relief crew is due to blast off on Tuesday to the crippled Mir space station, where it has to perform risky repairs and daring spacewalks crucial for the future of the world's only orbiting station.

Commander Anatoly Solovyov, 49, and 43-year-old flight engineer Pavel Vinogradov will fly to Mir aboard a Soyuz spacecraft from Baikonur cosmodrome at 1532 GMT for what may be the toughest assignment in Mir's 11-year-old history.

The station suffered its worst accident on June 25, when a supply ship pierced its Spektr scientific module during a manual docking manoeuvre. Cosmonauts had to unplug power cables leading from Spektr's solar panels as they rushed to seal the hole.

The accident deprived Mir of up to half of its power supply, forcing the crew to stop scientific experiments, a vital part of their space programme, and causing new power troubles as Mir's electric-powered solar orientation system malfunctioned.

Restoring power to the stricken craft is the main task of the new crew, which replaces the two tired and accident-prone Russians who have been on Mir for months. U.S. astronaut Michael Foale, who arrived later, is due to stay until September.
On August 20, the newly-arrived cosmonauts are scheduled to don spacesuits and enter Mir's punctured and airless Spektr module to try to re-attach the power cables.

They will install a new hatch door leading to Spektr with a "hermoplate" with hermetic connections for the cables from Spektr's three working solar panels. Experts have said the fourth panel, damaged in the crash, is unlikely to be repaired.
Vinogradov will open the hatch to Spektr. Experts say he may face dangerous chemicals or scraps floating around. Any puncture in his space suit could mean a swift death.
Solovyov said on Sunday he was "absolutely sure" he and his crew mate would be able to restore power to the stricken craft.

Russian and U.S. space officials have said that if the Russians fail to restore the power their mission could be Mir's last. Failure could mean the end of the cash-strapped Russian space industry's lucrative cooperation with the Americans.
President Bill Clinton's top science adviser said last week a new NASA astronaut would only be sent to Mir if his Russian colleagues can fix it.

A spacewalk in September would determine how to proceed with mending the hole in Spektr, Solovyov said on Monday. "Based on the results of our spacewalk on September 3, we will decide how to carry out the works and what kind of equipment we will need to seal the holed module," Solovyov said in a televised interview from the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan.
Solovyov said his crew would have limited tools and means to repair the station. The crew is due to perform a total of six spacewalks for inspection, repairs and scientific purposes.
The U.S. shuttle Atlantis may bring up extra equipment for repairs and Russian cosmonaut Vladimir Titov, who will fly on it, may also take part in a spacewalk to help out.
The Soyuz craft was placed on a launch pad on Sunday at Baikonur in preparation for Tuesday's launch.

"All of Soyuz's systems are now being checked. Everything is responding normally," said a spokesman at the Russian Military Space Forces. "The next important stage is fuelling the Soyuz-U booster rocket. But that will not happen more than three to four hours ahead of the launch," he added.

Solovyov and Vinogradov are expected to stay in orbit for about six months. Mission Control had previously entrusted repairs to the current crew, but became cautious after commander Vasily Tsibliyev developed heart troubles and decided to postpone the repair work after a vital computer was mistakenly unplugged. The two Russians are scheduled to return to Earth on August 14.
